glossary.Fever: Raised temperature from the hypothalamus resetting its set point, usually in infection; thermoregulation still works, unlike hyperthermia.
glossary.Frailty: Reduced physical reserve in older people, so small stresses such as cold or infection cause big decline.
glossary.Exertion: Hard physical effort, which generates a lot of body heat.
glossary.Seizures: Episodes of abnormal, excessive electrical brain activity, often causing jerking and loss of awareness.
glossary.Respirations: Breaths; slow respirations means a low breathing rate.
glossary.CNS: Central nervous system: the brain and spinal cord.
glossary.CNS dysfunction: Brain not working properly, such as confusion, seizures or reduced consciousness.
glossary.Heat dissipation: Getting rid of body heat, mainly by sweating and widening skin blood vessels.
glossary.Thirst perception: Feeling thirsty; it weakens with age, so older people drink less and dehydrate.
glossary.ECG: Electrocardiogram: a recording of the heart's electrical activity from skin electrodes.
glossary.Long QT: A prolonged interval from start of the QRS to end of the T wave, raising risk of dangerous arrhythmias.
glossary.Brisk reflexes: Exaggerated tendon reflexes, a sign of increased nerve excitability, e.g. in serotonin syndrome.
glossary.Tremor: Involuntary rhythmic shaking of a body part.
glossary.Dilated pupils: Pupils wider than normal, seen with serotonergic or stimulant drugs such as MDMA.
glossary.U&Es: Urea and electrolytes: a blood test of kidney function, sodium and potassium.
glossary.Glucose: Blood sugar; low or high levels can cause confusion and must be checked.
glossary.Warmed IV fluids: Fluids heated to about body temperature and given into a vein to rewarm and support circulation.
glossary.Perioperative: Around the time of surgery: before, during and after an operation.
glossary.Axillae: The armpits; large vessels there make ice packs effective for cooling.
glossary.Cold water immersion: Placing the body in cold water: the fastest way to cool a heat stroke patient.
glossary.Rehydration: Replacing lost body water, by mouth or through a drip.
glossary.Impaired consciousness: Reduced alertness, from drowsiness to coma.
glossary.Saline: Salt water solution (0.9% sodium chloride) used for drips and washouts.
glossary.Supportive care: Treatment that keeps the body going (fluids, oxygen, monitoring) while the cause is fixed.
glossary.Cardiac monitoring: Continuous ECG display to catch arrhythmias early.
glossary.Cardiac arrest: The heart stops pumping effectively, so there is no output and no pulse.
glossary.Shocks: Electrical defibrillation shocks given to restore a normal rhythm in VF or pulseless VT.
glossary.Cardiac conduction: The spread of electrical impulses through the heart that triggers each beat.
glossary.Repolarisation: The recovery of heart muscle cells' electrical charge after each beat, shown by the T wave.
glossary.Enzyme function: How well the body's protein catalysts work; they slow down in the cold and break down in heat.
glossary.Protein denaturation: Heat unfolding proteins so they stop working, killing cells.
glossary.Multi-organ dysfunction: Failure of two or more organ systems at the same time.
glossary.Cardiac output: Volume of blood the heart pumps per minute (heart rate times stroke volume).
glossary.Peripheral vasodilation: Widening of blood vessels in the skin and limbs, which drops blood pressure.
glossary.Serotonergic: Relating to serotonin, a brain and gut chemical messenger; serotonergic drugs include SSRIs and MDMA.
glossary.Metabolic heat production: Heat made by the body's chemical reactions and muscle activity.
